kept.title: 521 nets in 23 days, and the kind of training flipped twice
kept.claim: The project trained 521 value nets that were saved with weights. Up to the end of period 4 almost all were trained from scratch (285 of 331). In periods 5 and 6 short fine-tunes of an existing net took over (145 of 153). In period 7 the new content brought back training from scratch (20 of 29). The busiest stretch was period 3, the first three days with the owner away: 155 nets, about 52 a day.
kept.subset: Every runs/2026-* folder that holds a model.pt. 'Fine-tune' means the config names a parent net or a games count (scripts/finetune.py and family.py bursts). 'From scratch' means the config has n_train: scripts/learn.py in rounds of self-play, or the single-shot baseline trainings of 10-24 (P1, no rounds). Dated by created in run.json (local time).
kept.caveat: Five more run folders have no saved model (unfinished or failed) and are not counted. Periods differ in length (2 to 4 days); per day, P3 is still the busiest. The 8 P1 nets were single trainings, not rounds of self-play. The longest single training job was a fine-tune on 11-07 (0278-finetune, 3.95 hours on 3 threads); the one that used the most machine time was allcontent40k-s101 on 11-08 (3.4 hours on 6 threads, about 20 thread-hours).

kept.title: 4.4 million practice fights, a quarter of them on one day
kept.claim: The engine played 4,370,543 distinct practice fights to make training data, stored in 268 distinct datasets. 31 October alone produced 1,132,230 fights, more than periods 1, 2, 5, 6 and 8 together (1,082,768). Most of the data (3.57 million fights, 82%) came from round-0 pools that the search played with its hand-written heuristic. Only 0.80 million fights were played by a net, which is self-play in the strict sense.
kept.subset: Every datasets/<id>/manifest.json (n_games), counted once per distinct games file (games_sha256). This drops 17 byte-identical regenerated copies (104,069 fights) and the leftover daf87b2b715e.tmp folder. Each dataset is dated by the first run that trained on it; datasets no run used are dated by their file time.
kept.n: 268 distinct datasets, 4,370,543 fights
kept.caveat: A dataset counts once, on the day it was first used, even if later nets trained on it again. Copies whose games file is identical to an earlier one (the same seeds regenerated) are counted only once. Pools played by the heuristic are cheap and large (up to 240,000 fights). Sets played by a net are small (a few thousand per round).
kept.sources: datasets/*/manifest.json (n_games, games_sha256, parent_model), runs/*/run.json (created, datasets)
kept.reason: The dating method holds: I took each dataset's date from the earliest run.json 'created' that lists it, and used the file time for the 6 datasets no run used. That gives the miner's daily numbers exactly, apart from the double counts below. Two counting errors and one wording error. (1) 17 datasets are byte-identical copies of earlier ones (same games_sha256, for example five f-*-r0 sets of 3,237 games each and three pairs of 15,000-game heuristic pools). Together they add 104,069 fights that were counted twice. (2) datasets/daf87b2b715e.tmp is a leftover temporary folder (2,724 fights) that was counted as a dataset. After removing both: 268 distinct datasets and 4,370,543 fights. Heuristic or no-parent pools: 3,568,927 (81.7%). Net-played: 801,616 fights (0.80M, not 0.86M). 31 Oct: 1,132,230 fights. That is still more than periods 1+2+5+6+8 together (1,082,768). (3) The title says 'a third', but 31 Oct is 26% of all fights (it was 26% before the fix as well), so the title should say 'a quarter'. The changed days are 10-25, 10-31, 11-01 and 11-02. Two datasets have a file time later than their first use, which is a small problem with mtimes and doesn't affect the totals.

kept.title: The product's net was trained on 10-29 and has held the product role since 11-02
kept.claim: The product's net was trained on the evening of 29 October. (The real game on 14 November was played by another net, pack net seed 201, trained from scratch on 10 November on games with the real Act 1 cards.) Its family tree is short. A 60,000-fight pool played by the heuristic trained a first net. That net's 5,775 fights trained a second, whose 6,013 fights made up round 2. The seed-check run then retrained round 2 from scratch at three training seeds, and seed 1 became the product net. It learned from all 11,788 self-play fights plus a random sixth of the examples from the heuristic pool. On 11-01 two fine-tunes of it (burst8, then burst8hp2) took over for a day. On 11-02 it beat them on HP kept at the end of a run and became the product net, and none of the 383 nets trained after it has replaced it since. 167 runs started from it, trained on data it played, or used it to play.
kept.subset: Lineage from round.json parent_run and dataset manifest parent_model fields. Round-0 sampling from round.json window.round0_sample (1/6 for rounds 1 and up; seed_check.py retrains on the same window). Product history from configs/product.json 'previous' and the docs/decisions.md entries of 11-01 and 11-02. Later nets are runs with a model.pt whose run.json created time is after 10-29 22:32:39 (local time).
kept.n: 1 product net; 11,788 self-play fights + 1/6 of the examples from a 60,000-fight heuristic pool (+3,000 validation fights); 383 later nets (including its 2 seed siblings); 167 runs that refer to it directly (173 counting their descendants)

events.label: Round-0 pool: 60,000 fights played by the heuristic search (dataset 2bad7e)
score+branch-s0-r0 trains on half of that pool's examples
r0's 5,775 fights train score+branch-s1-r1, the first round of a night loop
r1's 6,013 fights are added and round 2 trains (with a sixth of the pool); the loop reaches round 10 by 06:55, about one round every 19 minutes
Seed-check retrains round 2 at seed 1 on the same data: the future product net
Fine-tunes of it take over: burst8 becomes champion, then burst8hp2 becomes the product
It beats burst8hp2 on HP kept at the end of a run and becomes the product net
Still the product net, now with the chooser and new search flags; 383 nets trained since 10-29
Plays the real game

kept.caveat: Seeds 101 and 201 of the same retrain are its siblings and are counted among the 383. Most later nets were experiments judged on their own yardsticks, not challengers. 'Not replaced since 11-02' means none passed the rule for becoming the product, not that every one played worse. The 1/6 sample is of examples spread across all 60,000 pool fights, so the pool still shaped it.
kept.sources: runs/2026-10-2[7-9]-*/round.json, run.json, config.json; datasets/{2bad7e15394f,47199f1023e9,b51c304673cb,eb96eb4a46c3}/manifest.json; scripts/learn.py d0_samples; scripts/seed_check.py round_window; configs/product.json; docs/decisions.md 'HP bonus promoted' (11-01) and 'Product net: the 10-29 net' (11-02)
kept.reason:
My own script reproduces most of the numbers. The four dataset manifests give 60,000 + 5,775 + 6,013 = 71,788 training games, plus 3,000 for validation. 383 runs with a model.pt were created after the product run's created time (10-29 22:32:39 local time); that count includes its own seed siblings s101 and s201. Exactly 167 runs name the product run or one of its datasets in their config, round or run files directly (173 if their own descendants are counted too). The timeline times also match: 10-27 21:28, 10-28 04:03 and 04:23, and r10 at 06:55, about 19 minutes per round.

Two parts are wrong:
(1) 'It learned from 71,788 fights' is not true. Round 2's window (s1-r2 round.json) has round0_sample = 1/6, and learn.py d0_samples uses that fraction for every round from 1 on. seed_check.py round_window checks that the retrain uses the same sample. So the net trained on all 11,788 self-play fights but only a random sixth of the examples from the 60,000-fight heuristic pool. That sixth is spread across all 60,000 games, so the 'fights' count overstates what it learned from.
(2) 'Never replaced it' is false. configs/product.json 'previous' shows burst8hp2-s1 (trained 11-01, a fine-tune whose recipe starts from the 10-29 net, per decisions 'Burst ratchet...') as the product from 11-01 to 11-02. Before it, burst8 s1 was the ladder champion. The 10-29 net only became the product on 11-02 ('Product net: the 10-29 net'), after beating burst8hp2 on end-HP. So it was briefly replaced by its own fine-tunes and won the role back. It has not been replaced since 11-02.
Period 3 (born 10-29) is right.

kept.title: More data helped, until 40,000 fights a group
kept.claim: The lab tested whether more training fights make a better net. Going from 5,000 to 20,000 fights per group raised the held-out won share by +0.011. Going from 20,000 to 40,000 added +0.009. Going from 40,000 to 80,000 (a 240,000-fight dataset, the biggest the project ever made) added only +0.003, and the two seeds disagreed (+0.024 and -0.019). On 1 November the lab stopped scaling data and kept the 20k default for experiments. 40k became the usual size for new from-scratch nets only from 8 November.
kept.subset: Round-1 nets on the tight2 bench, one turn deep, held-out half (12,200 fights per net). Won-share differences are paired by seed. Only n_train differs between arms.
kept.n: 5k vs 20k: 5 seeds; 20k vs 40k: 3 seeds; 40k vs 80k: 2 seeds
kept.caveat: The first step is a fourfold increase and the other two are doublings. With only 2 seeds at 80k, the flat result is weak evidence. Both 80k nets also failed the ladder against the 10-29 champion (-0.018, -0.024). The 80k training jobs took 2.9 hours (s1) and 1.0 hours (s101) on 6 threads. The 5k/20k/40k results were read on 31 October; the 80k results and the stop decision came on 1 November.

kept.reason: The three paired gains reproduce exactly from runs/*-data{5,20,40,80}k-s*-r1-*/round.json (gate.halves.held_out.net, n=12,200 each, paired by seed with the same train_seed and round0_seed). 5k to 20k: +0.0113 (se 0.0061, 5 seeds). 20k to 40k: +0.0087 (se 0.0032, 3 seeds). 40k to 80k: +0.0025, seeds +0.0244 and -0.0194. Datasets 9533627344f5 and 121978db780d hold 240,000 games each, the largest of the 286 manifests. One repeat needs care: data20k-s201 has two r1 folders, but 8836ba7 has no round.json (it never finished), so only 95c5a40 counts and nothing is counted twice. Two statements are wrong. (1) '40k stayed the size for from-scratch nets to the end' is false. The 11-01 decision says 'the default n_train stays', and the next nine round-0 runs used 20k (lean-* on 11-01 and 11-02). 40k became the usual size only from 11-08 (allcontent40k), and 20k and 5k runs still happened on 11-06 and 11-10. (2) 'Each 80k training took about 2.9 hours' is true only for s1 (job 0057a9a, 23:27 to 02:19). s101 (0057a9b) took 1.0 hours (02:59 to 04:02). Dating: the 5k/20k/40k reads ran on 10-31 (period 3), and the 80k runs and the stop decision came on 11-01 (period 4). Period 4 is acceptable if the stop is the headline. The claim no longer says only the data size changed, because the 5k step is fourfold; the caveat notes that.

kept.title: Fine-tunes on as few as 11 fights
kept.claim: In period 6 the lab mostly stopped training nets from scratch. Instead it fine-tuned one existing net in short bursts on new content's fights: 127 fine-tunes against 8 from-scratch runs. Of the 127 bursts, 94 used 99 fights or fewer, and 12 used just 11. The question had shifted from 'what is the best net?' to 'how few fights does the net need to adapt to new content?'.
kept.subset: Fine-tune runs created 11-06 to 11-09 (run.json created, local time) whose run.json has a parent net; the games value from each config.json. One memory-check rerun with an identical config (ycards-heur-g400-s1-memcheck) is left out.
kept.n: 127 fine-tune nets (one parent net); 8 from-scratch runs in the same days
kept.caveat: Burst sizes count fights of new content mixed into a 10,000-position replay pool, not the whole training set. The from-scratch runs in the same days used 5,000 or 40,000 training positions, a different unit, so the page doesn't compare the two. Small bursts are cheap, so many seeds and variants were run; that partly explains the counts.
kept.sources: runs/2026-11-0[6-9]-*/config.json (games, pool, n_train), run.json (created, parent)
kept.reason: I recomputed this from runs/*/run.json (created 11-06 to 11-09, local time) and config.json. 136 runs were created in that window. 128 of them have 'games' and the same parent net (runs/2026-10-29-seed-check-r2-s1-1a789b2/model.pt), and their bar counts match the miner's exactly. I found three errors. (1) The claim's arithmetic is wrong: 12+44+2+36 = 94, not 92. (2) One run is counted twice. 2026-11-07-ycards-heur-g400-s1-memcheck-457824d has the same config as 2026-11-07-ycards-heur-g400-s1-1dd4e45, including seed and game_seed, and the same datasets. It is a rerun to check memory three hours later, so the 400 bar should be 19 and n should be 127. (3) The '40,000 fights per group' comparison uses a different ruler. The from-scratch runs (allcontent40k-s1/s101, r0/r1, 11-08) have n_train=40000, which counts training positions (puzzles), not fights, and there is no 'per group'. The fine-tune 'games' count fights of new content mixed into a 10,000-position replay pool. The two numbers can't be compared as like for like. The 'mostly stopped training from scratch' part holds: the window has 8 from-scratch runs (4 ids5k with n_train 5000, 4 allcontent40k) against 128 fine-tunes. The bars chart fits the statistic.

kept.title: The three longest jobs ran 34 hours in one lane, far past their first estimates
kept.claim: The longest job in the queue's history is 0083-mutate-monsters: 13 h 56 min on 3 threads (11-04 03:24 to 17:21). It ran the two-turn product player on a stage-A table of mutated monsters, widened from 40x4 to 200x4. The second and third longest (0092, 10 h 11 min; 0113, 10 h 00 min) came from the same goal1-yardstick lane and followed it with gaps of 56 and 6 minutes. That lane kept 3 threads busy from 11-04 03:24 to 11-05 14:35. All three outran their first estimates (340, 450 and 330 min) by 1.4x to 2.5x. The steward raised each estimate mid-run from the job's pace, the last time when the job was 97-99% done. Short jobs (under an hour) usually finished in about half their estimate (median 0.50x, n=954).
kept.subset: jobs that started and ended; wall time from started to ended; first estimate = the 'from' of the first entry in the job's estimates list, or estimate_min if it was never revised
kept.n: 1,091 started jobs; the top 3 shown
kept.caveat: Wall time includes any slowdown from other jobs sharing the machine (other lanes ran alongside). The stored estimate_min is the last estimate, revised from pace near the end of each run, so comparing against it makes the estimates look accurate when they weren't. Three jobs is too few to say that long jobs are estimated worse in general.
kept.sources: jobs/done/0083-mutate-monsters.json, 0092-mutate-monsters.json, 0113-mutate-monsters.json (fields started, ended, threads, estimate_min, estimates)
kept.reason: The durations, threads, dates and totals all reproduce: 1,091 started jobs, 484.8 wall hours and 1,710 thread-hours. 0083 ran 836 min, 0092 ran 611 min and 0113 ran 600 min, all on 3 threads in lane goal1-yardstick. The claim that "their estimates held" is wrong, though. The miner compared each run against estimate_min, which is the last estimate, and the steward raised that number while the job was running, using the job's own pace. The 799 for 0083 was set at 787 of 836 minutes, with 197 of 200 starts done. The 607 for 0113 was set at 14:33, two minutes before the job ended. The first estimates were 340, 450 and 330 min, so the jobs took 2.5x, 1.4x and 1.8x those. Two smaller fixes: "back to back" leaves out a 56 min gap between 0083 and 0092 (and 6 min before 0113), and "held the machine" overstates it. Each job used 3 threads, and other lanes' jobs ran alongside (0087, 0095, 0143, 0151, 0152, 0154). The short-job figure holds: jobs under 60 min had a median of 0.50x their estimate, n=954. Their estimates were rarely revised, so their first estimate gives the same result.

kept.title: How long a job waited in the queue before it started
kept.claim: In period 5 the median job started 5.5 minutes after it was queued. In period 6, when family chains queued hundreds of reads at once, the median wait rose to 124 minutes, and one job in ten waited more than 4.7 hours. The longest wait in the queue's history was 30.6 hours: 0059l8b-bash, queued 11-01 15:48 and started 11-02 22:21. It was waiting for memory, not for another job: its 6 GB reservation never fit in the free RAM, and it started one minute after a manager cut the reservation to 3.5 GB.
kept.subset: started jobs; wait = started minus added; period by start time
kept.caveat: Part of each wait is deliberate. About 3 in 10 started jobs were queued to run only after another job (--after) or only if another passed (--if-passed). Others waited for their memory reservation to fit, so a wait does not only mean waiting for free threads. Periods 1 and 2 had no queue.
kept.sources: jobs/done/*.json (added, started, after, if_passed, note)
kept.reason: My own script reproduced every number. There are 1,224 done files and 1,091 started jobs, with unique ids and no duplicates. All timestamps are local time. Per-period counts, the medians (122.7, 17.8, 5.5, 124.4, 97.5, 30.7) and the 30.6 h maximum match exactly. My 90th percentiles (inclusive method) are 514, 213, 181, 280, 602 and 304. The miner's index method gives 528, 228, 183, 284, 607 and 304, which is the same picture, and P6's '4.7 hours' holds either way. In P6, 245 of 470 started jobs are family jobs, so the explanation for P6 is supported. One part is wrong: the cause of the longest wait. 0059l8b-bash has no 'after' and no 'if_passed' field. Its note says it waited because its 6 GB memory reservation could never fit in the free RAM. A manager lowered it to 3.5 GB at 22:20 on 11-02, and the job started at 22:21. The claim that it waited 'behind the jobs it was set to wait for' is therefore false. I fixed that sentence. The caveat is kept and widened: about 30% of started jobs carry after or if_passed, and memory reservations also delay starts.

kept.title: The machine did not sleep: busy threads by hour of day
kept.claim: The queue ran day and night. Between midnight and 08:00, it used 31.5% of all queue thread-hours, close to the 33.3% an even spread would give. Over the whole queue the quietest hour, 07:00, still averaged 3.7 busy threads against 5.5 at the busiest, 10:00. In period 3 the machine was busy around the clock (12 threads at midnight, 01:00 and 08:00). In period 5 the nights were the quiet part (about 2 threads, 1.6 to 2.3, from 22:00 to 04:00), while the long mutated-monster jobs ran in the day.
kept.subset: started jobs; each job's threads spread over the clock hours it ran; value = average busy threads in that clock hour for that period (thread-hours divided by the number of such hours the queue existed, 10-30 12:00 to 11-14 06:00)
kept.n: 1,091 started jobs, 1,710 thread-hours
kept.caveat: Threads are what each job declared, not measured CPU use. Work run outside the queue (training in periods 1 and 2, the real game, builds) is not counted. P3 covers only 10-30 12:00 to 10-31, and P8 ends with the last finished job on 11-14 06:07, so each of their cells averages over one or two days (P8's 07:00 to 23:00 cells come from 11-13 alone).
kept.sources: jobs/done/*.json (started, ended, threads)
kept.reason:
My own script reproduces every number exactly. It finds 1,091 started jobs and 1,710 thread-hours between 10-30 12:25 and 11-14 06:07, a night share of 31.5%, 3.7 busy threads at 07:00 against 5.5 at 10:00, and all 144 heat cells. Two sentences in the claim go further than the grid supports, so I corrected them.

1) Period 5 nights were not "under 2 threads from 22:00 to 04:00". The values are 1.6 at 22:00, 2.3 at 23:00, 1.7, 1.8 and 2.0 at 00:00 to 02:00, 1.9 at 03:00 and 2.1 at 04:00.

2) Period 3 was not "busiest overnight". It hit 12 threads at 08:00 as well as at 00:00 and 01:00, and it stayed high around the clock. Its 00:00 to 07:00 average (9.7) is barely above the rest of the day, and it covers only about 1.5 days.

The mutated-monster point holds. In period 5, mutate-monsters jobs made up 131 of the 216 daytime thread-hours.

The chart type fits. Hour-of-day by period is not the per-day chart already on the page.

kept.title: Why jobs failed, period by period
kept.claim: Of 1,224 jobs, 1,031 ended ok, 131 were cancelled before they started (20 of them automatically, because a job they depended on failed), 53 failed and 9 were killed, lost or ended without a status. The most common cause of failure was a missing file or module (14), often a job pinned to a code snapshot that lacked a file it needed. A test run found a fault 11 times (10 full-suite runs and one single test file), 6 of them in period 6. Out of memory struck in two bursts: three self-play learn jobs in period 3 and three in period 8, when the wide recipe's re-runs died one after another (0987, 0988, 0997) right after 0975 died of a stack overflow.
kept.subset: jobs/done with status failed; cause read by hand from each job's log tail, reason field and exit code; period by start time (added time for two jobs that never started)
kept.n: 53 failed jobs (P3 10, P4 4, P5 7, P6 11, P7 9, P8 12)

ys: input from an earlier job missing or bad
refused: control played with other settings

kept.caveat: The causes are a hand classification of the last error lines in each log, so a few could belong to a neighbouring group (0057a6i shares its log file with another job, so its cause can't be checked). A failed test run counts as a job doing its job. The 'refused' failures are the gauntlet's own guard stopping a comparison with a differently-played control, which is also a check working as intended. Most cells hold 0 to 3 jobs; read the grid as where failures happened, not as rates.
kept.script: python -I scratch/hist/machine/fails.py  (log tails), then extra2.py (cause by period table); jobs_stats.py status (cancel reasons). Checked by scratchpad/hist/verify/h-machine-failures/v.py
kept.sources: jobs/done/*.json (status, exit_code, reason, pin, note), logs/jobs/*.log tails
kept.reason: My own pass over jobs/done/*.json gives the same numbers: 1,224 jobs, of which 1,031 ok, 131 cancelled (20 with a "did not pass" reason that names a failed job they depended on, 111 with no reason), 53 failed, and 5 ended-unknown + 2 killed + 2 lost = 9. Failed jobs by start time (added time for 0005 and 0006, which never started): P3 10, P4 4, P5 7, P6 11, P7 9, P8 12. When I read the log tails and the reason field myself, every cell of the heat grid comes out the same. The exit codes back up the groups: 3221225725 = 0xC00000FD is a stack overflow (0975), and 1073807364 = 0x40010004 is the process ended by Windows (0565, 0908, 0927). The 0975 -> 0987/0988/0997 chain checks out in the job notes. Three wording fixes are needed. (1) Only one of the three out-of-memory failures in P3 was in teacher workers during distillation: 0049e's log shows a teacher. 0049d died building training rows in numpy, and 0052 died while generating tight fights, with no teacher in either log. (2) The "test suite found a fault" row holds 10 runs of the full suite (scripts/test_full.py) plus one single test file (0013, test_curriculum.py, P3), so "the full test suite found a fault 11 times" overstates it. Six of them in P6 is correct. (3) Of the 14 missing-file-or-module failures, only 0334 and 0432 clearly ran a pinned code snapshot taken before their script existed. 0117/0118 were pinned snapshots that lacked a config file. 0082/0084/0085/0086 were pinned jobs whose launcher (exec.py) could not find the program it was told to run. 0053/0054 lost the sts module while it was being rebuilt (sts.sts missing). 0005/0006 never started (WinError 2). So "often a pinned snapshot that lacked a file it needed" is accurate, and "before its script existed" is not. One more point: 0057a6i shares 0062-bash.log with another job, so its cause ("other") cannot be checked from its log. Nothing else to refute: there are no duplicate files (ids are unique), each row is a cause and each column a period, and the per-cell counts are shown as counts rather than presented as rates.

kept.title: What got measured when: training runs first, gauntlets from 1 Nov
kept.claim: The project changed which ruler it used. In periods 2 and 3 the measurements were mostly training runs (111 and 134). The paired ladder lived only from 30 Oct to 1 Nov (39 tests). From 1 Nov the 11-floor gauntlet took over (347 files), and from period 5 the mutated benches (167 files). Period 6, when real Act 1 went in, was the busiest stretch: 412 result files and training runs, against 32 in the final two days.
kept.subset: Training runs from runs/index.csv (by run date; 498 of the 535 run folders are indexed); ladder tests from results/ladder/log.jsonl; result files (.json, top level only) in results/<kind>/ by file modification time. 'other' = exact-puzzles, adapt, packs, gen_powers, depth_probe. It replayed the fatal fight of the 117 sequences no player had cleared. With 16 playouts per option it won 3 of them, and with 64 it won 7 (6%). Only 2 of those 7 were among the 69 boss fights (0 at 16 playouts). The other 5 were elites or hallway fights. On 30 boss fights the product had won, the rollout player lost 7 (16 playouts) and 3 (64 playouts). With 64 playouts, a fight took on average 5,300 playouts and 7 s on the lost set, and 7,700 playouts and 52 s on the won set. kept.claim: On 26 October the exact solver turned 2,000 near-the-end positions from close fights into puzzles and worked out the true value of every move. kept.title: Hexaghost and The Guardian were the run-killers
kept.claim: Across 58,546 lost gauntlet runs (duplicate files removed), Hexaghost ended 16,962 (29%), The Guardian 12,545 (21%) and Slime Boss 6,581 (11%). Together the three bosses ended 62% of all failed runs. In P4 to P7 a player who reached Hexaghost lost to him 33% to 38% of the time. In P8 The Guardian edged ahead, 28.7% against 27.1%. Slime Boss cost 10% to 14%, and each of the three elites only 3% to 6% of the fights against it.
kept.subset: 335 gauntlet files with distinct sequences (12 copy or rerun files dropped), all players mixed, one shape and rest 0.3; share of fights against each encounter that were lost, per period
kept.caveat: Each period mixes different players, decks and nets, so change across periods is not a measure of progress. P8 is small, about 1,400 fights per boss. The boss comes after a fixed rest, but elites come at whatever HP is left, so their lower loss rate partly reflects when they appear. Copies of the same results (sanity, thread and scale checks, a rerun) are counted once.

kept.reason: My own count from all 347 files matches every number the miner gave: 58,744 lost runs, 17,025 / 12,590 / 6,612 runs ended, 61.7%, fights per period, and every heat cell. There are two problems. (1) The title is false for P8. In P8 The Guardian beat Hexaghost on both measures: 28.7% of his fights lost against 27.1%, and 382 runs ended against 373. So Hexaghost was not the run-killer in every period. (2) 12 files are copies whose sequences repeat another file's exactly: 9 '*-sanity-*' files, the scale-t3/t8 pair, the thread-check pair, the lanes-e2e pinned/unpinned pair and the genpack '-cells-r2' rerun. They add 865 runs that are counted twice. Removing them changes the totals a little: 58,546 lost runs, Hexaghost 16,962 (29.0%), Guardian 12,545, Slime Boss 6,581, top three 61.6%. The cells move by at most 0.2 points. All files use the same shape (11 floors, boss last) and the same rest of 0.3, so the shape is not mixed. Players are mixed, and the caveat already says so. P8 is small (about 1,400 boss fights each), so do not read the P8 dip as a trend.
